about: Changing an object's tags without replacing them. Tags are a vocabulary shared across types rather than properties of one, so `set` cannot reach them and a whole-list write would destroy every tag the writer had not heard of.

cases.why: The whole reason this is not a whole-list write. A client that knows about one tag would send one tag, and a server treating that as the new set deletes the rest — the same failure `set` has, on the field most likely to be shared between tools.
Removal names what goes, never what stays. The mirror image of the case above and the same failure if implemented as a replacement.

A queue draining on a bad network sends the same write twice and hears the answer once. If a repeat were an error, every reconnect would surface failures for work that had already succeeded — and no tag is duplicated, because a tag list is a set.
The same argument from the other side. The state the caller asked for is the state that now holds, which is what idempotent means.

Tags and properties are separate namespaces and a write to one is not a write to the other. Worth pinning because the obvious implementation rebuilds the object, and rebuilding is where the property nobody modelled goes missing.

There is no reading of this that is obviously right, and choosing one silently is how a board ends up tagged the opposite of what somebody asked for. The same argument as two ids on a create: a contradiction is the caller's bug, and guessing hides it.
